clinicalPearls: Suspect the syndrome when peptic ulcers are multiple, refractory to standard treatment, in atypical sites (distal duodenum or jejunum), or recur after apparently adequate therapy
Secretory diarrhoea and steatorrhoea are common and may dominate the picture, driven by massive acid output that inactivates pancreatic enzymes
A markedly raised fasting serum gastrin together with elevated gastric acid output points strongly to the diagnosis
Acid-suppressing drugs elevate gastrin and should ideally be withheld before measurement, though safe withdrawal requires careful judgement in ulcer-prone patients
The secretin stimulation test provokes a paradoxical rise in gastrin from tumour cells and helps confirm the diagnosis in equivocal cases
Around a fifth to a quarter of cases arise within multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, so screen for hyperparathyroidism and pituitary disease
Most tumours lie within the gastrinoma triangle around the duodenum and pancreatic head and are frequently small and multiple
Somatostatin-receptor imaging such as gallium-labelled DOTATATE scanning has become central to locating primary and metastatic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Gastrinoma is a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour, usually arising in the duodenal wall or pancreas. Autonomous, unregulated gastrin release drives sustained hypersecretion of gastric acid and trophic expansion of the parietal cell mass. The resulting acid load overwhelms mucosal defences, producing severe and recurrent peptic ulceration, while the low intraluminal pH in the small bowel inactivates pancreatic lipase and injures the mucosa, causing diarrhoea and fat malabsorption. A substantial minority occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, and a significant proportion behave malignantly with regional nodal and hepatic spread.
additionalDifferentials: Retained gastric antrum syndrome after gastric surgery
Chronic atrophic gastritis with secondary hypergastrinaemia
Other causes of chronic secretory diarrhoea such as VIPoma
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum gastrin, ideally measured off acid-suppressing therapy
Gastric pH or acid-output assessment to confirm hyperchlorhydria
Secretin stimulation test to demonstrate a paradoxical gastrin rise
Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g. gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography) for localisation and staging
Cross-sectional imaging and endoscopic ultrasound to define primary tumour and metastases
Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone and pituitary screening to exclude multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
redFlags: Complicated ulcer disease with haemorrhage or perforation
Severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance from high-volume secretory diarrhoea
Hepatic metastases indicating advanced malignant disease
Features of coexisting multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 such as hypercalcaemia
Rapid symptom rebound on stopping acid suppression
reference.prognosis: Effective acid suppression with proton-pump inhibition controls symptoms in most patients, and complete surgical resection of localised sporadic tumours can be curative. Outlook is largely determined by tumour biology and the presence of hepatic metastases, with indolent disease often compatible with prolonged survival.
pitfalls: Attributing hypergastrinaemia to the tumour when it is actually driven by acid-suppressing drugs or atrophic gastritis
Dangerously withdrawing acid suppression to test gastrin in a patient at risk of ulcer complications
Overlooking multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and its associated hyperparathyroidism
Assuming a single tumour when duodenal gastrinomas are often small and multiple
Delaying somatostatin-receptor imaging and missing occult metastatic disease
management: Suppress the massive acid output with high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy to heal ulcers and control the secretory diarrhoea
Surgically resect localised sporadic gastrinoma, offering the prospect of cure after accurate localisation
Use somatostatin analogues for symptom and tumour control in unresectable or metastatic disease
For hepatic metastatic disease, consider peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, targeted agents and liver-directed treatments
Screen for MEN1 with serum calcium, parathyroid hormone and pituitary assessment, adapting management when disease is multifocal
Monitor fasting gastrin, chromogranin A and imaging for recurrence and progression
Provide genetic counselling and family screening in MEN1-associated disease
